The Smartphone Shakeup — Timeline chart race (2007–2026)

Chapters:
0:00 Intro — The stage is set: pre-iPhone incumbents and the smartphone boom
0:42 2007–2010 — iPhone appears, Samsung scales up
1:45 2011–2014 — Nokia slips, Android giants rise
2:30 2015–2019 — Huawei explodes to a 240M shipment peak (2019)
3:25 2020 — Pandemic and supply-chain shocks
4:10 2021 — Huawei collapse after sanctions; Xiaomi surges; Apple peaks
5:00 2022–2024 — Market realignment, the new top 3
5:40 2025–2026 (est) — Who’s coming back? Forecasts & takeaways
6:20 Outro — Subscribe for more chart races

Story summary:
From the iPhone's first 1.4M units in 2007 to an era where a single vendor ships 200+ million phones annually, this video animates two decades of winners, collapses and comebacks. We show real shipment figures (millions) for Apple, Samsung, Nokia, Huawei and Xiaomi from 2007 through 2026 (2024–2026 are estimates). Watch how Nokia — once dominant — falls to near-zero smartphone shipments after 2012, how Huawei climbed to ~240.6M units in 2019 then plunged after US sanctions, and how Xiaomi rose from zero to approach Samsung and Apple in peak years.

Sources & notes:
- Primary sources: IDC, Strategy Analytics, Canalys, company quarterly reports (annualized shipment figures)
- Specific milestone figures: Huawei ~240.6M (2019), Apple ~235M (2021), Xiaomi ~192.1M (2021)
- 2024–2026 numbers are labeled as estimates based on public supply/shipments trends and analyst consensus

instagram_caption:
🚀 The phone that rewrote the rules: inside the 20‑year smartphone war

In 2007 Apple shipped just 1.4 million iPhones. Fast-forward to 2019: Huawei peaks at ~240.6M phones — a meteoric climb that made it the world’s No.2 by shipments. But by 2021 Huawei was crushed by sanctions, falling from a 2019 high to roughly 36M units — one of tech’s most dramatic collapses. Meanwhile Nokia, once king, drops from tens of millions to near-zero smartphone sales as the market shifts to touchscreens and ecosystems.

This timeline shows real shipment numbers (millions) from 2007–2026 for Apple, Samsung, Nokia, Huawei and Xiaomi. Samsung grew steadily into a juggernaut (peaks above 320M in 2013–2014). Apple’s iPhone climbed in fits and starts — a big jump in 2015 (231M) and its highest recent shipment year around 235M in 2021. Xiaomi went from essentially zero in 2007 to ~192M in 2021 as a value-led disruptor that rode Android and aggressive global expansion.

The story is raw and clear: one vendor (Huawei) rocketed on low-cost flagship value and carrier deals, then imploded almost overnight when supply and software access were cut off. Another (Nokia) was slow to pivot to modern app-driven smartphones and lost the crown. Samsung and Apple adapted, diversified and kept shipping at scale. Xiaomi seized gaps in emerging markets and scaled quickly.

What’s next? By 2024–2026 our estimates show consolidation: Samsung and Apple hold the high end, while Xiaomi pushes growth and Huawei slowly rebuilds hardware volume. Nokia remains a minor player in smartphones but still exists as a brand.

Which move mattered most to you — the iPhone launch, Huawei’s rise, or Nokia’s fall? Drop your pick and why in the comments — I’ll pin the most insightful reply. Follow for weekly data-driven chart races and a deep dive on the next big tech flip.

Headline: The Smartphone Shakeup — How Nokia fell, Huawei soared and then crashed, and how Apple, Samsung and Xiaomi re‑wrote the market (2007–2026)

Detailed summary:
This visualization charts annual smartphone shipments (in millions) for five major vendors from 2007 through 2026 (2024–2026 shown as estimates). Key milestones: Apple’s introduction of the iPhone in 2007 (1.39M units) that sparked the modern smartphone era; Samsung’s steady scale-up into a market leader (peaking above 320M in the mid‑2010s); Huawei’s rapid rise to ~240.6M shipments in 2019 and its subsequent collapse following sanctions; Nokia’s slide from tens of millions to near-zero smartphone shipments after 2012; Xiaomi’s aggressive growth from virtually zero to ~192.1M in 2021.

Why it matters:
The chart tells a larger story about platform ecosystems, geopolitical risk, supply‑chain vulnerability and the power of scale and software. The winners adapted to app ecosystems and global carrier channels; the losers were slow to pivot or were cut off from essential supply and software partnerships.

Sources: IDC, Strategy Analytics, Canalys, company reports, and public analyst consensus for 2024–2026 estimates.
